title: Spring flow improved early June hypoxia forecasts after a level update and gave no clear seasonal gain in Chesapeake Bay in 2015-2025
abstract: We tested whether a published spring river-flow relation forecasts later Chesapeake Bay hypoxia. We fitted linear rules to 1985-2012 monitoring-based mainstem volumes below 2 mg/L dissolved oxygen, then tested 2015-2025. For the primary May-October average, the fixed January-May flow rule had RMSE 0.245 cubic miles, against 0.229 for the previous five-observation mean. Its MSE skill was -13.7%, with a conditional 95% three-year block interval of -107.6% to +56.0%. A recent level update reduced bias but gave skill of -0.1% [-65.8%, +47.1%]. The June-September average also had no clear gain. A secondary early June test gave a narrower positive result. Keeping the old slope and updating the recent level cut MSE by 44.4% [36.2%, 60.1%] in ten available years. Removing any one year left 41.9-47.0% gain. The conditional percentile band after adjustment for 22 outcome tests was 32.5-75.2%. Gains were also positive against a recent median; some other benchmark intervals included zero. Exploratory April-ending flow gave 34.9% gain. Few years, missing early June 2020, revised observations, sparse monitoring and conditional uncertainty limit inference. These are retrospective forecasts, not archived real-time tests. The package supplies original code, aggregate evidence, figures and exact external-source provenance. It tests a published relation, not the printed anoxia or nutrient equations.

display.caption: In 2015-2025, the old spring-flow slope with a recent level update reduced early June MSE by 44.4% against the previous five observations. It gave no clear seasonal gain. Thin bars are conditional 95% three-year block intervals. Wide light bars use Bonferroni percentile limits for 22 outcome comparisons. Early June has ten values; other displayed targets have eleven. This is a retrospective reconstruction.

Left: later fixed-rule MSE skill against a training mean and a recent mean. Right: flow slopes fitted in the old and later periods. Pointwise intervals use three-year blocks. May overlaps the predictor period and is not a future forecast. Sparse observations and wide later intervals limit inference.

The Lake Erie test motivates explicit observation versions and separates a water quality forecast from its physical interpretation.
Published positive spring flow relation and use of flow as a nutrient-load proxy. We test the relation with later broad-hypoxia estimates, not its printed anoxia equations.
Prior Chesapeake hypoxia forecasting, target choice and observation uncertainty. Its operational and nutrient models are not tested here.
Prior wind and climate analysis gives context for unmeasured later-season physical effects.
